catalogTitle: Purify Your נשמה Before Entering שבת (Intro. and beginning of מזמור לדוד הבו)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Mizmor LeDavid, the opening of Kabbalas Shabbos, as the completed harp of seven voices and as the border crossing into Shabbos, where a Jew must purify himself to be let in.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the two customs from Tzfas, the Ramak's Lechu Neranenah and the Arizal's Mizmor LeDavid, both now said, and explains that Mizmor LeDavid begins receiving the extra soul of Shabbos. Its three 'havu' and seven 'kol' match the ten utterances of creation: three upper levels and seven days of time. The seven voices are the seven notes; joined in harmony they make music, mismatched they are noise, and he contrasts holy Jewish music with music that arouses the animal in man. On the seventh day the harp is complete, so we begin to sing. He brings the Gemara that the eighteen names of Hashem in this psalm correspond to Shemoneh Esrei and its seven voices to the Shabbos Shemoneh Esrei. Finally, Mizmor LeDavid is the customs post between the weekday and Shabbos: one must do teshuvah and immerse, as one immerses to enter the Mikdash or Eretz Yisrael, or Shabbos will feel like a burden.

en: The Ramak's custom of opening Shabbos with Lechu Neranenah and the Arizal's of opening with Mizmor LeDavid were both accepted, and with Mizmor LeDavid one begins to receive the extra soul of Shabbos.
The three 'havu' and seven 'kol' of the psalm correspond to the ten utterances of creation: three upper levels beyond time and seven that became the days of the week.
The seven voices are seven notes: matched in harmony they are music, unmatched they are noise, and the Mashgiach contrasts holy Jewish music with music that brings out the animal in man.
The eighteen names of Hashem in Mizmor LeDavid are the eighteen brachos of Shemoneh Esrei, so on Shabbos one does not lose their blessing by not asking for one's needs.
Mizmor LeDavid is the customs post between the weekday and Shabbos, where the angels inspect whether a Jew comes with Torah, mitzvos and teshuvah.
Entering Shabbos requires purification through teshuvah and immersion, and someone who did not prepare is turned away and finds Shabbos a burden.

title.en: Opening Shabbos with Mizmor LeDavid

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Ramak's custom of Lechu Neranenah and the Arizal's of Mizmor LeDavid, and says Mizmor LeDavid starts the receiving of the extra soul of Shabbos. He then ties the psalm's three 'havu' and seven 'kol' to the ten utterances of creation and the seven days.

title.en: Seven voices as notes: harmony and noise

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven voices appear as the seven notes, which make music only when they match, like colors in a painting or a good shidduch. He contrasts holy Jewish music sung by tzaddikim and at Shabbos zemiros with music whose mismatched noise arouses the animal in man.

title.en: The harp is complete: we begin to sing

summary.en: On the seventh day the harp of seven notes is complete, so Kabbalas Shabbos begins with song; Lecha Dodi adds the Kallah, Malchus, and the Zohar speaks of the union of Shabbos. The Mashgiach notes that he blends what he took from sefarim with his own thoughts, and returns to the three 'havu' and seven 'kol' that together make ten.

title.en: Eighteen names, eighteen brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Berachos that the eighteen brachos of Shemoneh Esrei correspond to the eighteen names of Hashem in Mizmor LeDavid and the seven of Shabbos to its seven voices, and tells how the nineteenth bracha was added against the heretics. He concludes that on Shabbos one keeps the blessing of all eighteen brachos by resting and asking only for holy needs.

title.en: Crossing the border into Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes entering Shabbos as passing from the domain of the many, the sitra achra, into the domain of the One, and explains why the second day of creation lacks 'ki tov'. Mizmor LeDavid is the customs post where angels inspect a Jew, and just as one immerses to enter the Mikdash or Eretz Yisrael, one immerses to enter Shabbos.

title.en: A mikvah makes a better Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how a great man saw Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld going to the mikvah daily and heard from him that if a mikvah can make a gentile into a Jew, it can make a Jew into a better Jew. He adds that a gentile may not keep Shabbos, so a Jew must rid himself of the bit of the gentile in him before Shabbos.

title.en: Turned away at the border: preparing for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of bochurim for whom Shabbos was the hardest day, and explains that they were refused entry for lack of preparation. He says the whole week should prepare for Shabbos, reads 'Kol Hashem al hamayim' as the customs officer's first question, 'did you go to the mikvah?', and stresses that immersion without teshuvah does not help.

oneLiner.en: Learning the end of Tanya chapter one, the Mashgiach explains how the four bad middos of the animal soul come from the four elements, and why a Jew's animal soul, which comes from kelipas nogah, can be turned to holiness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the animal soul lives in the blood, which is why a Jew may not eat blood, and that the sitra achra imitates holiness the way a monkey imitates a man. Everything is made of four elements, fire, air, water and earth, which he explains with everyday examples such as a balloon, water that cannot hold a shape, and gravity. From the four elements come four bad middos: anger and pride from fire, which rises; pursuit of pleasure from water; wildness, mockery and idle talk from air, which has no substance; and laziness and sadness from earth, which always falls. He then explains that a Jew's good middos and his animal soul come from kelipas nogah, the 'shining' kelipah of Yechezkel's vision, which can be raised to holiness, like orlah fruit in the fourth year and the fourth layer at a bris milah. A Jew eats with brachos and washing; even a simple Jew's good deeds are inwardly for Hashem, while a gentile's are for himself.

en: The animal soul is in the blood, so a Jew may not eat blood, since what one eats becomes part of him.
All of creation is a combination of four elements: fire, air, water and earth, corresponding to the four letters of Hashem's Name.
Four bad middos come from the four elements: anger and pride from fire, pursuit of pleasure from water, wildness and idle talk from air, laziness and sadness from earth.
A Jew's animal soul comes from kelipas nogah, which can be turned to holiness, while that of a gentile comes from the three impure kelipos, which cannot.
A gentile's good middos are ultimately for himself, while a Jew, even a simple one, inwardly does good for Hashem.

title.en: The soul in the blood and the four elements

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the animal soul is in the blood and that a Jew therefore may not eat blood, and that the sitra achra imitates holiness. He introduces the four elements that everything is made of and explains air as something real that has no substance, like the air in a balloon.

title.en: Water, earth and fire

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains water as having substance but no stability, earth as solid, and fire as the energy in everything, including the warmth in a person. He notes that the nations call the four elements gas, liquid, solid and energy.

title.en: Anger and pride from fire, pleasures from water

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya's words that four bad middos come from the four elements in the blood. Anger comes from fire, as an angry face turns red; pride also comes from fire, because everything falls to the earth by gravity while fire alone rises. The craving for pleasures comes from water.

title.en: Wildness from air, sadness from earth

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that wildness, mockery, boasting and idle talk come from air, which has no substance, and illustrates with wild music that has no taste, contrasting it with real Chassidish song. Laziness and sadness come from earth, which falls fastest; a depressed person lies in bed and does not want to get up, while a joyful person rises fresh.

title.en: Kelipas nogah and the fourth year of orlah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that even the natural good middos of Jews, mercy and kindness, come from kelipas nogah, the weakest kelipah, which can go either to holiness or to impurity. He brings Yechezkel's vision of four barriers, the last being nogah, like a window shade the sun shines through, and the mitzvah of orlah: three years forbidden, the fourth year holy.

title.en: How a Jew eats

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts a rich gentile who eats breakfast in bed out of desire with an honest Jew, who first washes, says Modeh Ani, puts on tefillin and davens, then washes for bread and makes hamotzi. Through this the Jew turns his eating into holiness, which is possible because his animal soul comes from kelipas nogah.

title.en: Bris milah and doing good for Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the bris milah, where three layers are cut off and the fourth is raised through priah, to the four kelipos. He concludes that a gentile's good middos, even mercy, are for himself, while a Jew, even a simple one, inwardly does everything for Hashem, and a finer Jew eats in order to serve Hashem.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Mashgiach says that in a troubled time Jews need rachamim, and that even after open miracles and a Divine promise one must still daven, so perhaps one should not be so quick to skip Tachanun.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that the Jews, and the whole world, need rachamim (Divine mercy) now: things are boiling, and in September a separate state is to be declared, and no one knows what will come of it. He recalls that during the first intifada a rav arranged in his community that Avinu Malkeinu and V'hu Rachum be said every day. He then describes recent open miracles, such as a rocket that fell and did not explode while the other side wonders why; elsewhere such attacks cause great loss. Yet knowing that Hashem makes miracles does not exempt one from davening: Eliyahu HaNavi was told it would rain after three years of drought, and still he davened for it. The Mashgiach therefore suggests that perhaps one should not be so liberal about omitting Tachanun for yahrtzeits that do not truly concern us, especially on Monday and Thursday.

en: The Mashgiach says that the Jews and the whole world now need rachamim, since the situation is tense and no one knows what will come.
Hashem has shown great miracles, such as a rocket that did not explode, but knowing that miracles happen does not replace tefillah.
Eliyahu HaNavi davened for rain even after he was told that it would rain.
The Mashgiach suggests that perhaps one should not be so liberal about skipping Tachanun for yahrtzeits that do not truly concern us, especially on Monday and Thursday.

title.en: Rachamim, miracles and Tachanun

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the world needs rachamim in a tense time, tells of recent open miracles, and brings Eliyahu HaNavi, who davened for rain even after being promised it, to suggest that one should not be quick to skip Tachanun.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Akeidah was Avraham Avinu's greatest test because Hashem seemed far away and the command clashed with His promise, and that this test of serving Hashem with joy despite unanswered questions is the test of the last generation before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the custom of saying the Akeidah every day and explains that a nisayon is a test that raises a person, like a pupil's exam. Avraham's first test, being thrown into the fire for a G-d who had never spoken to him, seems greater than the tenth, when Hashem commanded him directly. The Mashgiach answers from 'he saw the place from afar': at the Akeidah Hashem felt distant, all of Avraham's levels were taken away, and he had questions, since Hashem had promised that his offspring would come through Yitzchak. Avraham went joyfully anyway, and even the simple answer, 'bring him up', was hidden from him as part of the test. Following the Ramban's principle that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, the Mashgiach says the last generation before Moshiach faces this same test of questions, as after the Holocaust. He closes with stories of the Lubavitcher Rebbe Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak's mesiras nefesh and defines mesiras nefesh as giving up one's will for Hashem's.

en: A nisayon is a test meant to raise a person, related to 'nes', a raised banner; each of Avraham's ten tests lifted him higher, and the Akeidah was the highest.
'He saw the place from afar' means that at the Akeidah Hashem was distant from Avraham: his lofty levels were taken from him and he felt like the simplest Jew of the generation before Moshiach.
Avraham's test at the Akeidah was having questions on Hashem, since he had been promised that his descendants would come through Yitzchak, and still going to serve Hashem with joy.
Following the principle that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, the last generation before Moshiach faces Avraham's test of questions.
Mesiras nefesh is not only giving up one's life; giving up one's own will for Hashem's will, even once a day or once a week, adds up to great mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The Akeidah daily and what a nisayon is

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the practice of saying the Akeidah every day to gain fear of Heaven, since every Jew carries something of Avraham and Yitzchak. He explains that a nisayon is a test that raises a person, like a pupil's exam, and connects it to 'nes', a raised banner; Avraham's ten tests ran from Ur Kasdim to the Akeidah.

title.en: The first test against the tenth

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Avraham reasoned his way to the Creator, defied Nimrod, was thrown into the fire and saved, and only then received his first prophecy. He asks why that first test, for a G-d who had never spoken to him, should be smaller than the Akeidah, which Hashem commanded him directly in prophecy.

title.en: He saw the place from afar

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers from 'he saw the place from afar': 'the place' is Hashem, and He was distant. With the example of a bachur who one morning learns and davens with feeling and another day cannot, he explains greater and lesser states of mind, and says that at the Akeidah all of Avraham's levels were taken from him.

title.en: The test of questions on Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the cause of the distance was that Avraham had questions: Hashem had promised that his offspring would come from Yitzchak. A Jew with questions strengthens his emunah and does not need to understand, as when he covers his eyes for Shema; Avraham went to the Akeidah with joy. The simple answer, that Hashem only said to bring Yitzchak up, was hidden from him as part of the test.

title.en: The fathers' test as a sign for our generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban's principle that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children, with the examples of Mitzrayim, and concludes that the last generation before Moshiach has the test of questions. He speaks of the Holocaust and the questions the heretics wrote, says that the survivors kept a stronger emunah, and that just as Avraham was blessed after the test, this generation will see great revelation. This, he says, is why the Akeidah is said every day.

title.en: The Lubavitcher Rebbe's mesiras nefesh

summary.en: Noting that tonight is the yahrzeit of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak of Lubavitch, the Mashgiach tells of his mesiras nefesh in Russia, his answer to the interrogator's gun, and how the Stoliner Rebbe, Rabbi Yisrael, stood up for him as a young man. He then explains that mesiras nefesh, needed in the time before Moshiach, also means giving up one's will for Hashem's, and that small acts of it add up.

title.en: L'chaim and blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls for l'chaim and blesses the bachurim that Hashem help them serve Him with joy and merit the coming of Moshiach. Singing follows.

catalogTitle: Ascribe Your Power and Accomplishments to Hashem (מזמור לדוד הבו פירושעל הפרק)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Mizmor l'Dovid Havu, the opening of Kabbalas Shabbos, as a call to ascribe every power, beauty and accomplishment in the world to Hashem, which is the meaning of resting from the 39 melachos on Shabbos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Mizmor l'Dovid Havu as the introduction to Kabbalas Shabbos: after six days of working and producing, a person must strengthen his emunah that everything comes from Hashem. 'Havu laShem bnei eilim' tells the powerful to ascribe their strength to Hashem. Going through the kapitel, he explains 'kol Hashem' as the Ten Utterances still hidden inside every force: the might of the ocean, of rulers, of beauty. One who sees Hashem in that power sweetens the din. The cedars that seem to block the heavens, like communist Russia, Yavan, Bavel and Rome, are broken by Hashem, so one should not panic before today's powers. Fire, the energy behind all four elements, is the same kol Hashem. Shabbos refutes man's claim to production: the 39 melachos, learned from the Mishkan, a miniature world, are the 39 curses after the sin, while Shabbos is blessing.

en: Mizmor l'Dovid Havu introduces Kabbalas Shabbos because after six days of production a person must strengthen his emunah that Hashem, not he, creates and provides everything.
'Havu laShem bnei eilim' calls on the powerful and respected to ascribe their strength and prowess to Hashem.
The 'kol Hashem' of the Ten Utterances is hidden in every force of nature and every human power, and a person must identify Hashem in it even where he cannot see Him.
Hashem breaks the 'cedars', the great powers that block the view of heaven, as history shows with Russia, Yavan, Bavel and Rome, so one should not panic before today's powers.
Shabbos is a refutation of man's claim that his own prowess and industry produced what he has.
The 39 melachos, learned from the Mishkan, are the activities Hashem put into the world and also the 39 curses given after the sin, while Shabbos is a day of blessing.

melachos as the curses of the sin

title.en: Havu laShem: ascribe your power to Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces Mizmor l'Dovid Havu as the preface to Kabbalas Shabbos: after six days of working a person must strengthen his emunah that everything comes from Hashem. He explains 'bnei eilim' as the powerful and respected, who must ascribe their strength to Hashem and bow before Him.

title.en: Kol Hashem in the waters and in every power

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'kol Hashem al hamayim' as the Ten Utterances concealed in the force of the oceans and 'kol Hashem bakoach' as the power hidden in kings and rulers, citing the Nefesh HaChaim. He tells of a Rav who, fleeing the Nazis, kept in mind that their power was only Hashem's, and explains that recognizing this sweetens the din.

title.en: Beauty, cedars and looking up to heaven

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'kol Hashem behadar' and 'shover arazim': the cedars symbolize mighty rulers like communist Russia, broken overnight. He explains why people look up to the sky for Hashem, brings the Gemara about davening in a room with windows, and shows how the cedars of a forest block the view of heaven, as Russia forbade belief.

title.en: Hashem breaks the cedars of Lebanon

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows from history that Hashem breaks the cedars: Yavan, which made a god of beauty and might, and Bavel, Greece and Rome all vanished. He says one should not panic before today's powers, and explains 'vayarkidem kmo egel' as Hashem moving the boundaries of nations like a restless calf.

title.en: Flames of fire and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'kol Hashem chotzev lahavos eish': fire is energy, the strongest of the four elements, and all energy in the world is the kol Hashem from the six days of creation. From here he explains Shabbos as a refutation of man's belief that his own prowess produces, and as the day of menuchah when one realizes Hashem did everything.

title.en: The 39 melachos learned from the Mishkan

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Shabbos one testifies that Hashem created the world by refraining from the 39 melachos with which He made it. Since no one witnessed creation, these are known from the Mishkan, a miniature world, whose work is detailed in the parshiyos of Terumah and Tetzaveh and defined in Maseches Shabbos, the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch.

title.en: The melachos are curses; Shabbos is blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the 39 melachos are 39 curses: before the sin bread and clothing grew on trees, and the Mishnah's melachos are the toil of producing bread and clothing that came with the curses. Shabbos is blessing, so it has no melachos; in the future, as the Gemara says, the land will again produce without work. He closes that one must bow to Hashem and proclaim that all power comes from Him.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that permitted food comes from kelipas nogah and holds sparks and souls that a Jew elevates by eating it properly with a brachah, and from the Tanya's first chapter he contrasts a Jew's good middos, which can be l'shem shamayim, with the kindness of the nations, done for their own honor.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews that opposite the holiness there are four kelipos: three impure ones that cannot be transformed, and kelipas nogah, which can be turned to good. A Jew's blood and middos come from nogah, a non-Jew's from the three impure kelipos; likewise forbidden foods come from the impure kelipos and permitted foods from nogah. A Jew who eats as a Jew should, with a brachah, calmly and l'shem shamayim, elevates the food. He tells how the Yismach Moshe once ate a dish rag without noticing, explains the sparks and souls hidden in foods, why fish need no shechitah, and how thanking Hashem for the taste He gave food is itself a brachah. After a story of a young tzaddik who sold brandy, he urges bachurim to make brachos with meaning, warns about non-kosher food, and closes with the Tanya's first chapter on the source of a Jew's good middos and the self-serving kindness of the nations.

en: Opposite holiness stand three impure kelipos that cannot be transformed and kelipas nogah, which can be turned to good; a Jew's blood and middos, and all permitted food, come from nogah.
A Jew who eats as a Jew should, with a brachah, calmly and for the sake of Heaven, turns the food to good and brings it into holiness.
Every food holds sparks of holiness and parts of souls waiting for a tikun, and by hashgachah pratis each portion reaches the person whose soul is connected to it.
There are many levels of eating; the simple level is to eat l'shem shamayim in order to be healthy, without overeating, and to thank Hashem for the good taste He gave the food.
Non-kosher food becomes part of a person's body, so the Mashgiach calls for great care in kashrus.
Following the Tanya's first chapter, a Jew's natural good middos come from the body and kelipas nogah and can be done for Hashem, while the kindness of the nations is done for themselves.

title.en: Kelipas nogah and eating like a Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the four kelipos: three impure ones that cannot be transformed and nogah, which can. A Jew's blood and middos and all permitted foods come from nogah, while forbidden foods come from the impure kelipos; a Jew who eats with a brachah, calmly and l'shem shamayim, elevates his food.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe's supper

summary.en: The Mashgiach says it is good to watch how a tzaddik eats, since the greatest tzaddikim do not even know when they eat. He tells how the Yismach Moshe, left to take supper alone, ate soapy dishwater with a rag in it, thinking it was meat, because his mind was on high kavanos.

title.en: Sparks and souls in food; fish and meat

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that since the shattering of the vessels, sparks of holiness and even souls are scattered in everything, and a brachah such as borei nefashos gives them their tikun. Souls of tzaddikim with a small blemish go into fish, so fish need no shechitah or salting, while meat needs shechitah, removal of fats and veins, and salting before only nogah remains.

title.en: Eating l'shem shamayim and the gift of taste

summary.en: The Mashgiach says not everyone can eat like the Yismach Moshe; the simple level is eating l'shem shamayim to stay healthy, without overeating or too much sugar. Hashem could have made man run on gasoline like a car, yet He gave food taste and color, as the Mashgiach sees in a fruit store; thanking Him for that is itself a brachah, the meaning of feeding the world with chein.

title.en: Honest eating and hashgachah pratis in food

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how an honest Jew eats: healthy food, a treat on Shabbos or at a simcha, a bite with coffee when weak, but not cake just because it smells good. By hashgachah pratis each portion, half an apple shared with a friend or a bottle of wine for Shabbos, holds souls connected to the one who eats it, waiting for his brachah before and after.

title.en: The brandy seller and a word to bachurim

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns that eating without thought brings a descent instead of an ascent, and tells of a great tzaddik who as a young man sold brandy and told a customer who drank without a brachah that it was his father's yahrzeit. He then tells bachurim that they need not eat like the Yismach Moshe, but must eat like Jews: a brachah with its meaning, knowing the taste is from Hashem, and a brachah acharonah.

title.en: Non-kosher food and the kindness of the nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that non-kosher candy brings the impure kelipos into the body and becomes part of it, so in that respect it is worse even than chillul Shabbos, and kashrus needs great care. He then contrasts a non-Jew's charity, given for publicity or out of natural pity, with a Jew's, which deep in his heart is for Hashem.

title.en: Tanya chapter one: the Jew's good middos

summary.en: Reading the Tanya's first chapter, the Mashgiach explains that a Jew's natural mercy and kindness come from the body and kelipas nogah, which is the secret of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil; he tells how Adam should have waited to make wine for kiddush. The nations' good deeds, per the Etz Chaim and the Gemara on 'chesed le'umim chatas', are done for their own honor, a fault that has crept into fundraising among Jews too.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Mashgiach speaks of the custom to say Tikunei Zohar from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Yom Kippur, seventy expositions on the word Bereishis through which Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rectifies Jewish souls.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by speaking of the special worth of a sefer that a tzaddik learned from, as opposed to the Sefer Chassidim's warning about a sefer from which a wicked person learned. He then turns to a custom among ovdei Hashem to say Tikunei Zohar from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Yom Kippur; he stresses that no one is obligated, and notes that the printers divided the sefer into a portion for each of the forty days. The Tikunei Zohar, he explains, is seventy expositions on the word Bereishis, and it is a preparation for Rosh Hashanah. Through it Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rectifies Jewish souls in these days, and since all Jews are bound to one another, those who say it help everyone. He closes with the wish that all merit to be rectified and to return to Bereishis, binding themselves to the Ribono shel Olam, and says that one must constantly strengthen oneself in these great days and not let them pass empty.

en: There is a custom among ovdei Hashem to say Tikunei Zohar from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Yom Kippur, though the Mashgiach stresses that no one is obligated.
The printers divided the Tikunei Zohar into a portion for each of the forty days.
The Tikunei Zohar is seventy expositions on the word Bereishis and serves as a preparation for Rosh Hashanah.
Through the Tikunei Zohar, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rectifies Jewish souls in these days.
The Mashgiach says one must constantly strengthen oneself in these great days and not let them pass with nothing.

the worth of a tzaddik's sefer

title.en: Tikunei Zohar: rectifying souls in Elul

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the worth of a sefer a tzaddik learned from, then of the custom to say Tikunei Zohar from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur: seventy expositions on Bereishis, a preparation for Rosh Hashanah through which Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rectifies Jewish souls. He closes with a l'chaim and a call to strengthen oneself in these days.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the generation before Moshiach, when the Satan pours out new temptations, small acts of emunah and self-guarding are precious in Heaven, and the greatest danger is the 'kiss' of the nations' culture.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that ours is the generation of the footsteps of Moshiach, when the trials are so hard that small deeds, like holding back a joke or not looking where one should not, give Hashem more pleasure than the great self-sacrifice of earlier generations; he illustrates this with the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the king and the talking parrot. He then teaches that the one mitzvah that carries everything is emunah, through a story of souls who demanded to know their purpose, and explains that emunah means never saying 'if only' (volt), since everything is hashgachah pratis. David's silence before Shimi's curse made him the fourth leg of the Divine chariot, because Shimi became the ancestor of Mordechai and Esther, and Purim defeats Amalek, which equals 'doubt'. The Satan, sensing his end, creates new temptations such as television, the internet and cell phones, as the Kohen Gadol needed a miracle on Yom Kippur. Esav's kiss teaches that today the nations bite with friendliness, so bachurim must distance themselves from goyish culture, sports and foods.

en: In the generation before Moshiach the trials are so great that small acts of restraint are worth more in Heaven than the great deeds of earlier generations.
The one mitzvah on which everything stands is emunah, and true emunah means not saying 'if only' about what happened.
Everything, including when and how much a person earns, comes through hashgachah pratis, Divine providence over each detail.
Before Moshiach the Satan is in an emergency, so he creates ever new temptations, and the yetzer hara of today is many times stronger.
Today the nations 'bite with a kiss': their friendliness draws Jews into their culture, and this requires a far greater guarding than in earlier generations.

title.en: Small deeds in the last generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach says this is the generation of the footsteps of Moshiach, when the trials are so hard that small deeds, like holding back a joke at lunch or not looking in the street, outweigh the great deeds of earlier generations. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the king who listened to a talking parrot rather than to his wise men.

title.en: The souls' demand and the mitzvah of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites the Gemara that Chabakuk based all the mitzvos on one, 'the tzaddik lives by his emunah', and tells a story from a disciple of the Ba'al Shem Tov: souls sent down again and again went from angel to angel demanding their purpose, until they were told that keeping the one mitzvah of emunah would spare them returning. Emunah, he adds, means truly believing and not saying 'volt'.

title.en: What 'volt' means: the late breakfast

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'volt' with a parable of a man who missed a lucrative business appointment because there was no milk for breakfast and blamed his wife. The real failure is the 'if only', since everything, how much and when a person earns, is hashgachah pratis from Heaven.

title.en: David, Shimi and the fourth leg of the chariot

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Shimi ben Gera cursed David as he fled from Avshalom, and David stopped Avishai from killing him, saying Hashem had told him to curse. At that moment it was decided in Heaven that David would become the fourth leg of the Divine chariot, with Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, and the Mashgiach asks why this act earned it.

title.en: Shimi, Purim and Amalek as doubt

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that Shimi was the ancestor of Mordechai and Esther, so by sparing him David merited Purim, the defeat of Amalek that completes Hashem's Name and throne. Amalek equals 'safek', doubt, the opposite of emunah, and David's faith that someone else would have cursed him anyway is what made him a leg of the throne.

title.en: The Satan's emergency and the new temptations

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that for thousands of years the natural yetzer hara from the sin of the Etz HaDaas sufficed, but before Moshiach the Satan has created television, the internet and cell phones. Like a wrestler who is losing, a woman who carried her piano out of a fire, a dying man or a candle that flares before going out, the Satan, knowing he will be slaughtered when Moshiach comes, summons new strength.

title.en: Why the Kohen Gadol needed a miracle

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah in Pirkei Avos that the Kohen Gadol never became impure on Yom Kippur, and the Tosfos Yom Tov's question why this needed a miracle after he stayed awake all night without eating. The answer is that all of Klal Yisroel's atonement depends on him, so the Satan concentrates on him; so too the Satan concentrates on our generation, which needs a far greater guarding.

title.en: Esav's kiss: biting with friendliness

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Esav wanted to bite Yaakov but his neck became like marble, and asks why Esav then kissed him; the answer is that when he could not bite with a bite, he bit with a kiss. For hundreds of years the nations kept Jews in ghettos, but now they are friendly, and that friendliness, through their culture, internet and cell phones, is the bite of the kiss.

title.en: Distance from goyish culture, sports and food

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the friendliness of recent popes and of the nations leads to intermarriage, and says one must distance oneself from everything goyish: following ball teams, eating pizza, eating turkey on Thanksgiving. Jews have their own foods for Shabbos and Yom Tov, and he closes that the responsibility to bring Moshiach rests on the bachurim of this generation.

catalogTitle: An Explanation of the Medrash on these Pesukim (ה' למבול ישב... יברך את עמו בשלום)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara Rashi brings on the last pesukim of Mizmor l'Dovid, that the nations feared a second Mabul at Matan Torah, showing that the inner life of water is Torah and that Hashem's 'thundering' in history is all for Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara in Zevachim that Rashi brings on 'Hashem lamabul yashav': at Matan Torah the nations, wise in astrology, saw the heavens arrayed as at the Mabul and ran to Bilaam, who told them Hashem was giving Torah to His people. To explain it he teaches that everything has a body and a soul, the Dvar Hashem that constantly recreates it; the soul of rain is Torah, which is why on Shemini Atzeres, the day of the neshamah, Klal Yisrael asks for Geshem. The generation of the Mabul refused the Torah that Noach, the neshamah of Moshe, should have given, so they received the outside of the water as a flood, while Klal Yisrael received its inside in forty days at Sinai. He ties 'bashalom' to the letter shin and to Shabbos, the day of Torah. Following the Radak, he reads the psalm as Hashem thundering on the nations before Moshiach, and closes with the Zohar's reading of the ayalah and the snake: the suffering of the galus will bring the birth of Moshiach.

en: According to the Gemara Rashi brings, the nations saw the heavens arrayed as at the Mabul during Matan Torah, feared a new flood, and Bilaam told them Hashem was giving Torah to His people.
Everything has a guf and a neshamah: the Dvar Hashem that recreates it every moment, and the neshamah inside every drop of rain.
The inner meaning of rain is Torah, which is why the request for Geshem is placed in Musaf of Shemini Atzeres, the highest point of the year.
The Mabul was the outside of the water given as punishment to a generation that refused the Torah; Klal Yisrael received the inside, the Torah, in forty days at Sinai.
Torah is bound to the number three, and 'bashalom' with its shin alludes to the Torah coming down like rain; this links the psalm to Shabbos, the day of Torah.
All of history and nature turn on one axis, the good of Klal Yisrael, and the suffering of galus is like the snake's strike that brings the ayalah to give birth to Moshiach.

title.en: The nations fear a second Mabul

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the last pesukim of the psalm and brings the Gemara in Zevachim cited by Rashi: the nations, great in astrology like Pharaoh, saw the heavens arrayed as at the Mabul during Matan Torah and ran to Bilaam, who told them Hashem was giving Torah to His people.

title.en: Every creation has a body and a soul

summary.en: As a first introduction the Mashgiach explains that everything has a chomer and a tzurah: the Dvar Hashem recreates the world every moment, unlike a carpenter whose table outlives him, and inside every drop of rain is a neshamah, the Dvar Hashem that makes things grow.

title.en: Geshem on Shemini Atzeres: rain as Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Shemini Atzeres as the center point around which all the chagim circle, and asks why its Musaf is devoted to asking for Geshem. He answers that the inner meaning of water is Torah, reads dagan, tirosh and yitzhar as halachah, aggadah and sod, and ties oil, the eighth, to what is above nature.

title.en: Noach, Moshe and the waters of the Mabul

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that the generation of the Mabul refused the Torah, and from the Gemara and the Zohar that Noach carried the neshamah of Moshe and should have given it. Because Noach did not daven for his generation the flood is called 'mei Noach'; Moshe, replanted in the generation of the desert, davened with mesirus nefesh and succeeded. The flood was the outside of the water the generation would not receive.

title.en: Matan Torah, the number three and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Matan Torah repeated the Mabul, forty days for forty days, but as the inside of the water; this is what the nations sensed and what Bilaam told them. He brings the Gemara in Shabbos on the threefold Torah, the Maharal on three as the center, the shin of tefillin and mezuzah, and reads 'bashalom' as the shin of Torah coming down like rain. He ends that Shabbos is the day of Torah, so the psalm leads into Kabbalas Shabbos.

title.en: The Radak: Hashem thunders on the nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Radak's reading of the psalm: before Moshiach, Hashem thunders on the nations, the 'wicked waters' that oppressed Klal Yisrael, breaks the proud cedars and makes them jump like a calf. From the desert of Kadesh, where the old generation passed and a new one rose, he concludes that all of nature and history turn on the good of Klal Yisrael, as will be seen when Moshiach comes.

title.en: The ayalah, the snake and Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Medrash that the ayalah cannot give birth until a snake strikes her, notes that such aggados (like Rabba bar bar Chana's) hold secrets, and gives the Zohar's explanation: the ayalah is Klal Yisrael, the snake is the suffering inflicted by the nations, and that suffering brings the birth of Moshiach. He closes that this seventh 'voice' is linked to Shabbos, a taste of the days of Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: Learning the opening of Tanya chapter two with bachurim, the Mashgiach explains how the Jewish soul, 'truly a part of G-d above', stays pure in its innermost point and comes from Hashem's own thought, which no created mind can grasp.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews Tanya chapter one: a Jew has an animal soul from kelipas nogah, which can be elevated when he eats for the sake of Heaven, and a G-dly soul, the subject of chapter two, 'truly a part of G-d above'. He shows this inner point through the Rambam's explanation of why a man forced to say 'I want' brings a valid korban, and through the Ramban's reason for forty lashes: the forty days of a child's formation, of which the first point never sinned, so only thirty-nine are given. The same point appears in the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur. He explains 'vayipach' as blowing from one's innermost depth, tied to the shofar, and the soul as coming from Hashem's thought and wisdom. Through the mashal of a watch and its maker, and of the five senses, he shows that a creation cannot understand its Creator. He closes with the Tanya's question of why souls differ in level, leaving the answer for next time.

en: The animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, so permitted things done for the sake of Heaven are turned to holiness, unlike the three impure kelipos.
According to the Rambam, every Jew has a spark of holiness that truly wants Hashem's will; beating only weakens the evil inclination, so his 'I want' is true.
The Ramban ties forty lashes to the forty days of a child's formation; since the first point of the soul never agreed to the sin, only thirty-nine are given.
'Vayipach', blowing, means bringing out breath from one's innermost being, which shows that the soul comes from Hashem's inner self.
The souls of Jews come from Hashem's thought and wisdom, which is one with Him and cannot be understood by any created mind.
A creation cannot understand its Creator, just as a watch cannot understand its maker, not for lack of intelligence but because it is a different realm entirely.

title.en: Two souls and kelipas nogah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews Tanya chapter one: the animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, so kosher food eaten for the sake of Heaven is elevated, while the three impure kelipos cannot be. He then opens chapter two, the G-dly soul, 'truly a part of G-d above'.

title.en: The Rambam on 'rotzeh ani'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the halachah that one who refuses to bring his korban is beaten until he says 'I want', and the Rambam's answer: every Jew's good inclination truly wants, and the beating only weakens the evil inclination. He then introduces the Torah's forty lashes, of which only thirty-nine are given.

title.en: Forty days of formation and the untouched point

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that forty lashes correspond to the forty days of a child's formation, and explains why only thirty-nine are given: the first point, the G-dly soul, never sinned. He finds the same in the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, the day of that point.

title.en: Vayipach: blowing from within

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's proof from 'vayipach be'apav nishmas chayim' and contrasts blowing with speaking: blowing comes with force from one's innermost self. He connects it to Rosh Hashanah and the shofar, to 've'atah nefachtah bi' in the morning blessing, and to the Zohar that one who blows, blows from within.

title.en: Souls from Hashem's thought and wisdom

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the world was created for the sake of man, who arose first in Hashem's thought, and that like a child drawn from the father's mind, Jewish souls are drawn from Hashem's wisdom. With the Rambam that Hashem and His wisdom are one, and the mashal of a watch and its maker, he shows why this is beyond understanding.

title.en: Not like our thoughts: the picture and the niggun

summary.en: From 'ki lo machshevosai machshevoseichem' the Mashgiach argues that more intelligence would not help a creation understand its Creator. He gives the mashal of a man who says he heard a beautiful picture or saw a niggun: each thing is grasped only by its own faculty.

title.en: Five senses and the bat

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that our whole contact with the world comes through five senses, a small number, and that some creatures, like the bat that senses its surroundings by sound in a dark cave, have senses we lack. Even with a million senses, he says, a person would not understand Hashem, because he is the watch and Hashem is the watchmaker.

title.en: Back to the Tanya: why do souls differ?

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Mashgiach reads the Rambam that Hashem is the knower and the known, beyond human grasp, and repeats that Jews come from the 'mind of the Father'. He then raises the Tanya's question: if all souls come from Hashem's thought and Hashem is One, why are there souls of the Avos and Moshe Rabbeinu and souls of the lowest generations? He leaves the answer for the next shiur.

oneLiner.en: On the yahrtzeit of Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen, the Mashgiach brings his teaching that a Jew shows where he belongs when, in a time of danger, he flees to the Ribono shel Olam.

abstract.en: At a l'chaim on the yahrtzeit of Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen, whose sefarim, the Mashgiach says, we learn as his talmidim, he says that one should say Tachanun in these days even on a yahrtzeit, because the Jewish people need a great yeshuah. Hashem has shown miracles, but one must still ask for rachamim. He then brings a teaching of Rabbi Tzadok on a Mishnah about a creature whose status is in doubt, whether it belongs to the land or to the sea: when it is chased it flees to dry land, and that is the sign that it belongs to the land. From this Rabbi Tzadok learns that in a time of danger a Jew flees to the Ribono shel Olam, and that shows where he belongs.

en: The Mashgiach says one should say Tachanun in these days even on a yahrtzeit, because the Jewish people need a great yeshuah.
Hashem has shown miracles, but one must still ask for rachamim.
Rabbi Tzadok learns from a Mishnah about a creature of doubtful status that a Jew shows where he belongs by fleeing to the Ribono shel Olam in a time of danger.

title.en: Fleeing to Hashem in a time of danger

summary.en: On Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen's yahrtzeit the Mashgiach says Tachanun should be said even on a yahrtzeit, since Jews need a yeshuah, and brings Rabbi Tzadok's teaching from a Mishnah that a creature flees to where it belongs, as a Jew in danger flees to Hashem.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to bachurim at the end of Shovavim on Shabbos Shekalim, the Mashgiach explains that guarding the holiness of the bris is the foundation that brings a bright Shabbos, true Torah, emunah and the light of the four parshiyos, and that a Jew's holy words become the shekalim offered above.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Shabbos Shekalim falling at the close of the six weeks of Shovavim. Milah, the first mitzvah given to Avraham Avinu, is called yesod; through it one merits the Name of Hashem, as hinted in the initials and final letters of 'mi ya'aleh lanu hashamayma' and in the Name written at a bris. Bereishis hints at the sixth middah, that of Yosef HaTzaddik, which leads to Shabbos. He urges bachurim to know the relevant halachos once, briefly, ties difficulties in emunah to lack of guarding, and tells those who struggle to speak with an ehrlicher Yid and not despair. Through the wonders of animals and the lion that bowed to the Divrei Chaim he shows the power of the tzelem Elokim, with two stories. He speaks about guarding speech, teshuvah, the light of the four parshiyos, and ends with the Pri Tzaddik: the words of Parshas Shekalim become the shekalim for Michael's offerings above.

en: Milah, the first mitzvah given to Avraham Avinu, is called yesod, the foundation of Yiddishkeit, and through guarding it one merits the Name of Hashem.
The middah of the bris is the sixth middah, Friday, which leads into Shabbos; through it one merits a bright Shabbos and bright tefillos.
Difficulties in emunah and in reaching the true Torah come from lack of guarding; one who struggles should speak with an ehrlicher Yid and never fall into despair.
A person who keeps his tzelem Elokim is feared by the animals; one who blemishes the kedushas habris loses it.
Guarding the mouth is part of guarding the bris, and emunah and milah, both from Avraham Avinu, go together.
Following the Pri Tzaddik, when Jews say Parshas Shekalim with holy speech, their words become the shekalim with which the offerings are brought above.

title.en: Milah, yesod and the end of Shovavim

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Shabbos Shekalim at the close of Shovavim and explains that milah, the first mitzvah, is called yesod and brings one to the Name of Hashem, as hinted in 'mi ya'aleh lanu hashamayma' and in the Name written at a bris. Bereishis hints at the sixth middah, of Yosef HaTzaddik; he urges bachurim to know the halachos briefly and says this middah brings a bright Shabbos and tefillah.

title.en: Emunah, struggle, and the tzaddik

summary.en: The Mashgiach says difficulties in emunah come from lack of guarding the eyes, thoughts and limbs, and that our generation's tests are harder. One who struggles should speak with an ehrlicher Yid, not despair, and ask Hashem for help; only through kedushah is one sure of the true Torah. He explains why Yosef alone is called tzaddik and how yesod leads to malchus, as Friday leads to Shabbos.

title.en: The wonders of creation and how to look

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the Divrei Chaim went to a zoo, and explains that seeing Hashem's creatures with the right thought brings one to awe: the lion's strength, the long-beaked birds, the giraffe's neck, the duck's webbed feet. He brings the Rambam on checking an animal's signs, and distinguishes between a glance and gazing.

title.en: The tzelem Elokim and the animals

summary.en: The lion bowed to the Divrei Chaim, which the Mashgiach explains through the passuk that the fear of man is on all animals, and through Daniel in the lions' den: an animal does not harm one who keeps his tzelem Elokim, while blemishing the bris loses it. He tells of a tzaddik who saw an ox climbing the stairs, and the Skulener Rebbe's account of wolves that sniffed a family and left.

title.en: Guarding speech, emunah and teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns bachurim against improper talk, says guarding the mouth and the bris are one matter, and links emunah with milah, both from Avraham Avinu; today both are the great tests. He promises that guarding brings a happy life, and says teshuvah is always possible, as the weeks of Shovavim show, though it is far easier while one is still clean.

title.en: The four parshiyos and Michael's offerings

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the four parshiyos correspond to the four letters of Hashem's Name and that tzaddikim felt great light in them, which one feels only when clean. He explains the shekalim that bought the communal offerings, and brings that even after the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed, the angel Michael offers korbanos above; the question is asked where the money for them comes from.

title.en: Words that become shekalim

summary.en: Bringing the Pri Tzaddik, the Mashgiach tells the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, whose word filled a valley with gold coins, and explains that likewise the words of Jews reading Parshas Shekalim become shekalim above that buy the offerings. Such speech must be holy, which comes from guarding oneself; he closes with a brachah for the building of the Beis HaMikdash.

catalogTitle: פסוקי דזמרה Destroys The Barriers that Block our תפילה . Explanation of the לשם יחוד Before ברוך שאמר (Intro to פסוקי דזמרה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why later generations need a longer davening, such as Pesukei d'Zimra and the added L'shem Yichud, and what L'shem Yichud means: uniting the hidden and the revealed aspects of Hashem against the concealment of Amalek.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that the Gemara treats Pesukei d'Zimra, like Maariv, as less than a full obligation, yet today it is accepted as one. He compares this to the question put to the Tzemach Tzedek: why are we stricter in kashrus than the Gemara and Rishonim? The answer, from the Tanya, is that food holds sparks of kedushah that eating must extract from the tumah around it; earlier generations were holier and could do this with foods we cannot. In the same way our davening grew longer, and the L'shem Yichud before Baruch She'amar was added. He explains its simple meaning: Hashem is one, but is perceived above as Havaya and below as the Shechinah, and every mitzvah aims to unite them with love and fear. Amalek hides Hashem's presence, which is why His name is hidden in the Megillah. Every mitzvah joins the hidden and the revealed, and a Jew must see Hashem behind the mask.

en: Pesukei d'Zimra, which the Gemara does not treat as a strict obligation, has become an obligation today because Klal Yisrael accepted it.

Food contains sparks of kedushah bound up in tumah, and eating with the Torah's process and with kavanah extracts them; earlier, holier generations could do this with foods later generations cannot, which is why later poskim are stricter.
For the same reason later generations need a longer davening, and the L'shem Yichud before Baruch She'amar was added.

Hashem is absolutely one, but He is perceived above as Havaya and in Klal Yisrael as the Shechinah, read as Adnus; the avodah of every mitzvah is to unite the two, and it needs both love and fear of Hashem.
Amalek works to hide Hashem's presence in this world, so the Megillah, which deals with hester panim, hides Hashem's name, yet His hand shows through at every turning point.
The Mashgiach says a Jew should identify Hashem in every event that happens to him or in the world, and not be blinded by the mask.

title.en: Pesukei d'Zimra becomes an obligation

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Gemara mentions Pesukei d'Zimra but does not seem to make it a strong obligation, yet today it is accepted as one, like Maariv, which the Gemara calls optional. He then introduces the question once put to the Tzemach Tzedek about why later poskim are stricter than the Rishonim.

title.en: Sparks of kedushah in food

summary.en: Answering from the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that food holds sparks of kedushah bound in tumah: forbidden food cannot be refined, while kosher food can, through shechitah, salting and a brachah with kavanah. The greater the kedushah, as in bread, the greater the tumah around it; earlier generations were holier and could refine foods that later generations must avoid.

title.en: A longer davening and L'shem Yichud

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the same idea to davening: later generations need a longer tefillah to purify themselves, and parts were added in recent centuries, among them the L'shem Yichud said before Baruch She'amar. He brings Rebbe Elimelech on its power, notes that it is Kabbalah but that every level of Torah also has a pshat, and sets out to explain it simply.

title.en: Uniting Kudsha Brich Hu and the Shechinah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem is absolutely one, but is perceived in different levels: above as the name Havaya, and dwelling in Klal Yisrael as the Shechinah, read as Adnus. All avodah aims to unite the two, and like every mitzvah this needs love and fear of Hashem, the two wings that lift a mitzvah up.

title.en: Yud-Kei, Vav-Kei and Amalek's concealment

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains uniting Yud-Kei, which belongs to the upper world, with Vav-Kei, Hashem's revelation in this world. Amalek is the head of the forces that hide Hashem, which is why the name and throne are incomplete in the war with Amalek, and why the Megillah, set in a time of hester panim, does not mention Hashem's name.

title.en: Hashem masked in the Megillah and in history

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'HaMelech' in the Megillah hints at Hashem, that the Megillah has no open miracles yet its events click together into one great nes, and that Hashem's name hides in the initial and final letters at its turning points. He adds that today too one can see Hashem in history, as everything in the world revolves around Klal Yisrael and Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Mitzvah as Yud-Kei Vav-Kei; removing the mask

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows through the At-Bash letter exchange that the word mitzvah is Yud-Kei, hidden, with Vav-Kei, revealed, so every mitzvah is a yichud. L'shem Yichud is said in the name of all Klal Yisrael, as a declaration to oneself of why one does the mitzvah. He ends with the avodah of Adar: to recognize Hashem in every event and rip off the mask, as on Purim.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter two with bachurim, the Mashgiach uses the mashal of steam, water and ice to explain how all Jewish souls are one part of G-d above even though they stand on countless levels, down to the low souls of the generation before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews that a Jew's body and animal soul come from klipas nogah, which can be raised to holiness, while a non-Jew's come from the three impure klipos. He illustrates this with a Midrash on 'uri tzafon uvo'i teiman': the nations can bring only olos, but a Jew can bring shelamim, which are eaten, because only a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven. Turning to Tanya chapter two, he explains that the second soul is a part of G-d above, yet souls range from Atzilus down to Asiyah, and he brings the Ba'al HaTanya's question how such levels can exist if all come from the One. His answer is a long mashal of water in a boiling kettle: invisible vapor, visible steam, water and ice are all the same water, changed on the way down. He applies this to the four worlds, the extra souls of Shabbos, warm and cold davening, the souls rooted in Adam HaRishon's head, heart, hands and heel, and our generation, the 'heel' before Moshiach, whose efforts are precious to Hashem.

en: A Jew can bring a shelamim, which is eaten, while a non-Jew can bring only an olah, because only a Jew, whose body comes from klipas nogah, can eat for the sake of Heaven.
The second soul of a Jew is a part of G-d above, yet souls stand on many levels, from Atzilus down to Asiyah.
Vapor, steam, water and ice are all the same water; the hotter it is the more spiritual and the higher it rises, the colder the more physical and the lower it falls.
So too all souls come from one root and one place, and only on the way down do some become coarser.
All souls were once part of Adam HaRishon's soul, and each draws its nature from its place in him: head, heart, hands or heel.
Our generation is the 'heel' before Moshiach, with low souls that cannot daven as earlier generations did, yet their struggle to serve Hashem is very precious to Him.

title.en: Why a non-Jew cannot bring a shelamim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that a Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah and a non-Jew's from the three impure klipos. He brings a Midrash on 'uri tzafon uvo'i teiman' and explains it: a non-Jew may bring only an olah, which is burned entirely, but not a shelamim, which is eaten, because only a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: A part of G-d above, on many levels

summary.en: Opening Tanya chapter two, the Mashgiach explains that the second soul is a part of G-d above, yet there are souls from Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, as one sees in any beis medrash. He then brings the Ba'al HaTanya's question: if every soul is a part of the One G-d, how can there be levels?

title.en: The mashal of the boiling kettle

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes water boiling in a kettle: invisible vapor at the spout, white steam rising, water falling back, and ice in the freezer. All are the same water: the hotter, the more spiritual and higher; the colder, the more physical and lower.

title.en: Four worlds and the souls from each

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the mashal to the worlds Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah and to the souls that come from each, from the Avos, Moshe Rabbeinu and the Ba'al Shem Tov down to the lowest souls. All come from one root and only change form on the way down; even Asiyah has nefesh, ruach and neshamah.

title.en: Extra souls of Shabbos; warm and cold Nishmas

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the points in the Shabbos davening where one receives the extra nefesh, ruach and neshamah. He then states the answer to the Tanya's question with the water mashal, and speaks of davening Nishmas cold like a snowball or warm like a hot glass of coffee.

title.en: Souls from Adam HaRishon's head, heart, hands and heel

summary.en: Reading the Tanya on the countless levels of souls, from the Avos and Moshe Rabbeinu to the generations of ikvesa dimeshicha, the Mashgiach brings a Midrash that all souls were part of Adam HaRishon. Head souls are drawn to the mind, heart souls to song and poetry, hand souls to mitzvos and tzedakah, and the lowest come from the heel.

title.en: The heel before Moshiach, and davening in Karlin

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that our generation is the 'heel' of Moshiach and contrasts davening today with earlier generations, telling of a misnaged who davened in Karlin with Reb Aharon Karliner. He closes that the generation of the Exodus were head souls while we are heels, yet the struggle of such small souls is very precious to Hashem.

oneLiner.en: At a lechaim, the Mashgiach describes Parshas Ki Seitzei and the days of Elul as a time of tikkunim for souls, and then speaks of the thanks owed to Hashem for being let into Yerushalayim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by calling Parshas Ki Seitzei a parsha full of tikkunei neshamos, corrections for souls, and mentions a tradition from earlier tzaddikim to learn the Sefer HaTikunim in Elul, a time of tikkunim. He says one should come close to such a time and let oneself be repaired. He compares this to the hilulah of a tzaddik, where saying lechaim is itself a tikkun for the tzaddik's soul, and says the parsha and the Shabbos, which draws from the parsha of its week, are tikkunim too. He mentions the Koritzer and speaks of asking for truth, and touches on the haftaros after the Three Weeks becoming a tikkun. In the second part, after wishing a good morning, he speaks of the great thanks owed to the Ribono shel Olam that, after nearly two thousand years, Jews are let into Yerushalayim, and says one must know what Yerushalayim is.

en: The Mashgiach calls Parshas Ki Seitzei a parsha entirely filled with tikkunei neshamos.
He cites a tradition from earlier tzaddikim to learn the Sefer HaTikunim in Elul, because Elul is a time of tikkunim.
Saying lechaim at the hilulah of a tzaddik is a tikkun for the tzaddik's soul.
Each Shabbos draws from the parsha of its week, so the Shabbos of a parsha of tikkunim is itself a tikkun.
The Mashgiach says one should thank the Ribono shel Olam greatly that, after nearly two thousand years, Jews are let into Yerushalayim.

title.en: Ki Seitzei and Elul as a time of tikkunim

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Parshas Ki Seitzei a parsha of tikkunei neshamos, brings the tradition of learning the Sefer HaTikunim in Elul, and explains that a lechaim at a tzaddik's hilulah, the parsha and its Shabbos are all tikkunim. He mentions the Koritzer and asking for truth.

title.en: Thanking Hashem for entering Yerushalayim

summary.en: After wishing a good morning, the Mashgiach speaks of the great thanks owed to the Ribono shel Olam that Jews are let into Yerushalayim after nearly two thousand years, and says one must know what Yerushalayim is.

oneLiner.en: Beginning Tanya chapter three for bachurim, the Mashgiach explains how a Jew can eat in holiness, then lays out the ten sefiros as ten powers in a person, from chochmah and binah to chesed, gevurah and tiferes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews that every Jew has two souls. A gentile's animal soul comes from the three impure klipos, so he may only bring an olah, while a Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah and can be raised to holiness: he can eat for the sake of Heaven and thank Hashem even for the taste. He illustrates the higher level of tzaddikim who did not feel taste at all with a story of the Yismach Moshe and his gabbai. Turning to the G-dly soul, he explains nefesh, ruach and neshamah as service in deed, speech and thought, and opens Tanya chapter three: each is made of ten levels. To explain this he describes the ten sefiros through which Hashem created the world and the matching ten powers in man. He explains chochmah as a flash of insight and binah as building on it, chesed as love and reaching out, gevurah as holding back, and tiferes as a beautiful blend of colors. He closes with the Lubavitcher Rebbe, teshuvah before Moshiach, and a personal story of a blessing he received from him.

en: Because a Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah, it can be turned to holiness, so a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven, unlike a gentile who may only bring an olah.
The Mashgiach says one should eat calmly, with the intention to be healthy for learning and davening, and thank Hashem in thought even for the taste of the food.
Nefesh, ruach and neshamah are the powers with which a Jew serves Hashem through deed, speech and thought, and each of them contains ten levels.
Hashem created the world with ten sefiros, and man, made in the image of G-d, has ten corresponding powers: three intellectual ones and seven middos.
Chochmah is the first flash of an idea and binah is the structure a person builds on it.
Chesed is love that reaches out to another, gevurah is the opposite, holding oneself in, and tiferes is the harmony of a blend.

title.en: Eating in holiness: a Jew and a gentile

summary.en: The Mashgiach announces the start of Tanya chapter three and reviews the two souls. A gentile's animal soul from the three impure klipos lets him bring only an olah, while a Jew can eat in holiness, with a brachah and calm, thanking Hashem in thought for the taste.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe and his gabbai

summary.en: The Mashgiach says great tzaddikim ate only for the sake of Heaven and did not even feel the taste, and tells how the Yismach Moshe's gabbai served him every course on one plate without his noticing. He adds that this level is not ours, but everyone can eat for the sake of Heaven and thank Hashem for the taste.

title.en: Nefesh, ruach and neshamah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the G-dly soul: nefesh, ruach and neshamah, received at the bris, at bar mitzvah and later through learning Gemara, serving with deed, speech and thought. He reads the opening of Tanya chapter three, that each has ten levels, and begins to explain it through the ten utterances and the ten sefiros.

title.en: The ten sefiros; chochmah and binah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the word sefirah from the sapphire stone, names the ten sefiros, and says man in the image of G-d has ten matching powers, the mochin and the middos. He explains chochmah as a sudden flash of insight while learning and binah as the building a bachur makes on it into a whole pshat.

title.en: Chesed, gevurah and tiferes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains chesed as love that reaches out and gevurah as holding back, linking them to Avraham and Yitzchak and to the first two brachos of Shemoneh Esrei. He explains tiferes as a beautiful blend, using white and red, mixed colors and the colors of a field or a sunset, and calls it the trait of Yaakov.

title.en: The Lubavitcher Rebbe and a broken heart

summary.en: Over l'chaim the Mashgiach speaks of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, who brought teshuvah down to the world as a drizzle before Moshiach's downpour, and tells how the Rebbe, unprompted, named the passuk 'lev nishbar' that the Mashgiach had been saying with tears for a sick relative. The shiur ends with l'chaim and brachos.

catalogTitle: Every Word a Silver Coin (Intro to פסוקי דזמרה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that every word of Pesukei d'Zimrah is a silver coin to be counted slowly, explains why true tefillah is dveikus that the soul needs as much as Torah, and why such tefillah is so hard in a generation the Satan is fighting for his life.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the teaching that Pesukei d'Zimrah should be said slowly, like a man counting silver coins, and brings the Magen Avraham that it should take half an hour. He describes people who davened for hours: a Chabad chassid in Williamsburg and the upstairs room of the Tzemach Tzedek shul in Yerushalayim, and the Ba'al HaTanya's letter about an hour and a half for Shacharis. Real avodah shebalev is dveikus, so one who has it cannot leave a word. He brings the Gemara that people deride tefillah, then the dispute whether Torah or tefillah is greater, and explains that they are brain and heart: the neshamah needs both to live. A sinner's heart is clogged; a passed test brings a good davening. Today tefillah is hard because the Satan, sensing Moshiach, fights with inventions and spiritual contamination. Yet this generation was sent on a shlichus to stay faithful in enemy territory, and he closes with the Shabbos before Tu B'Shvat.

en: Pesukei d'Zimrah should be said slowly, like counting silver coins, since every word is a coin; the Magen Avraham says it should take half an hour.
Avodah shebalev is not just understanding the words but dveikus to Hashem, and one who davens that way davens slowly because he cannot part from each precious word.
The Gemara says tefillah stands at the heights of the world, yet people deride it.
Torah and tefillah are like the brain and the heart: both are vital, and the neshamah needs tefillah as much as it needs Torah to stay alive.
A good tefillah is hard today because the Satan, seeing that Moshiach is near, fights for his life through new inventions and spiritual contamination.
Every person in this generation was placed here on a shlichus to remain faithful to Hashem amid these conditions, and that is what will bring the geulah.

title.en: Every word a silver coin

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the teaching that Pesukei d'Zimrah should be said slowly, like a man counting silver coins, and brings the Magen Avraham that it should take half an hour. He explains that Pesukei d'Zimrah is one unit framed by two brachos, and mentions tzaddikim who spent much longer.

title.en: Those who davened all day

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls a Chabad chassid in Williamsburg who davened Shacharis on Shabbos until the afternoon with tears, the upstairs room of the Tzemach Tzedek shul for those who davened all day, and the Ba'al HaTanya's letter that weekday Shacharis should take at least an hour and a half. He laments that today people mock such davening, and defines avodah shebalev as dveikus.

title.en: Torah or tefillah: which is greater

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who davens with real kavanah cannot leave a word he treasures, and asks why people praise long learning but deride long davening, bringing the Gemara that people make light of tefillah. He then brings the dispute whether Torah or tefillah is greater and how it bears on turning a shul into a beis medrash, and explains that the word tefillah means attachment.

title.en: The brain and the heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Torah to the brain and tefillah to the heart: among the 248 limbs some are vital and some not, and since a person cannot live without either, the question which is greater matters only for the halacha. He notes that some tzaddikim davened fast because they were purified, but ordinary people must toil until tefillah touches the heart, and one must merit a good tefillah.

title.en: A clogged heart and the king's daughter

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that just as the heart's vessels can clog, a sinner's heart is clogged and his davening becomes lip service, while passing a test brings a good davening. He tells the parable of the man who killed a dangerous serpent and won the king's daughter, who is tefillah, and with her access to the King.

title.en: The Satan's last battle: inventions

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the footsteps of Moshiach the Satan, sensing his defeat, fights harder. For thousands of years, from Noach's plow and Adam's fire, there was no progress, and only in the last two hundred years came an explosion of inventions that enslave people, take away their peace and, through the internet, destroy homes. Like a candle that flares before it goes out, this is the Satan fighting for his life.

title.en: A contaminated world, and why we are here

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that minds and hearts are hampered today because the spiritual atmosphere is contaminated, mirrored by polluted air, water and food, and that the radio shows how every word, of Torah or otherwise, fills the atmosphere. He asks whether we should complain to Hashem, and answers that every neshamah is placed in its time, place and family for a reason, to prove itself despite the conditions.

title.en: The shlichus of our generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that this generation was chosen for a shlichus no other generation had, like the best soldiers sent to the most dangerous front, to fight the yetzer hara wherever it is and remain faithful, which will bring the geulah. He closes by speaking of the coming Shabbos before Tu B'Shvat as a landmark from which the year climbs toward Purim, Pesach and Shavuos.

oneLiner.en: At a lechaim in memory of Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, the Mashgiach speaks of the Torah institutions across America that he planted and of his uncompromising truthfulness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach says people already felt that Reb Shraga Feivel was a special, lofty neshamah. He points to the hundreds of institutions of Torah and yiras Shamayim, chadarim and Bais Yaakov schools, throughout America, all planted by him, including Torah Umesorah, which he founded, and what he built in the yeshivah. He describes him as an ish emes who could not tolerate pretense: he did not want to be called Rabbi Mendlowitz but Mister Mendlowitz. The Mashgiach mentions that the Ponevezher Rav spoke at his hesped, and that Reb Shraga Feivel insisted on davening slowly, asking after davening what the rush was. He then raises a difficulty on the Gemara's teaching that even if the whole world says one is a tzaddik, one should consider oneself otherwise, since the Gemara elsewhere holds that what people say is so. He closes asking that his merit protect all of Klal Yisrael.

en: Hundreds of Torah institutions, chadarim and Bais Yaakov schools across America were planted by Reb Shraga Feivel.
The Mashgiach describes Reb Shraga Feivel as an ish emes who could not bear pretense and refused to be called 'Rabbi'.
Reb Shraga Feivel insisted on slow davening and asked after davening why people rush.
The Mashgiach asks how the Gemara can say to disregard the whole world calling one a tzaddik, when the Gemara elsewhere treats what people say as true.

title.en: Reb Shraga Feivel: builder and ish emes

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the Torah institutions across America that Reb Shraga Feivel planted, his refusal to be called 'Rabbi', and his slow davening, then asks a question on the Gemara about the whole world calling one a tzaddik.

oneLiner.en: Before Shabbos Zachor and Purim the Mashgiach explains that reading Parshas Zachor weakens the inner force of Amalek, the yetzer hara, and that Purim is a day of hidden, exalted kedushah to be spent in seriousness, prayer and closeness to Hashem, not in drinking and smoking.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining that everything has an inner life-force, and that Amalek's inner force is the yetzer hara that cools a Jew's emunah. Amalek cannot be fought with weapons, but reading Parshas Zachor weakens that force; it will be erased completely only with Moshiach. He asks the one reading and the listeners to have in mind to fulfill the mitzvah, links the war on Amalek to teshuvah and to coming properly to davening on Shabbos, and stresses Hodu at Minchah of Erev Shabbos. He then turns to Purim: the three days before it are like the days of preparation before Shavuos, Yom Kippur is only 'like Purim', and on Purim Hashem shows love to the lowest Jew and gives to whoever stretches out his hand. Purim's kedushah is so high that Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah. He warns at length against getting drunk and smoking on Purim, and closes urging the bochurim to daven on time.

en: Amalek's inner force is the yetzer hara that cools emunah, and reading Parshas Zachor weakens that force even though Amalek cannot be fought physically.
Until Moshiach comes Amalek can only be weakened, as Yehoshua only weakened him; his full erasure belongs to the time of Moshiach.
The remedy for the Amalek within a person is teshuvah, and part of it is coming properly to davening on Shabbos and not talking or wandering during Hodu.
On Purim Hashem shows love to even the lowest Jew, and just as one gives to everyone who stretches out his hand, Hashem gives to whoever asks.
Purim's kedushah is higher even than Shabbos and Yom Kippur, so it is a day of serious joy with trembling, not of mockery and smoking.
Purim's kedushah comes from a level above the name Havayah, which is why Hashem's name appears in the Megillah only hidden in initial and final letters.
The Mashgiach says that, practically, it is better not to get drunk or smoke on Purim, since many become alcoholics and smokers precisely from Purim.
